extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evidentiary criteria courts use on motions for preliminary injunctions in patent litigation, covering public acquiescence, defendant admissions/estoppel, proof of title, proof of intended infringement, and the relative weight of different types of proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence as evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence, in reference to this subject, is a voluntary submission, against interest, to an asserted right, which in the absence of a trial at law may alone often take its place in establishing, or presumptively establishing, the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May be shown by exclusive possession and exercise after grant; manufacture and repeated sale; selling rights to others; and public acquiescence in the patentee's exclusive exercise. Cited examples: Orr v. Littlefield; Potter v. Muller. Acquiescence is received as evidence on applications for injunctions and may rank next to judgments as a basis for presumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive possession and enjoyment strengthens the title
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive possession and enjoyment of the exclusive right for a term of years, without any successful impeachment of its validity, is usually regarded as sufficient to warrant an injunction to restrain infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may be manufacturing and selling repeatedly, granting rights to others, or long undisputed use. Courts consider such possession aided by the presumptions arising from the patent itself. Cases: Tappan v. National Bank Note Co.; Potter v. Muller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes in which public acquiescence is manifested
rubrics_metrics.description: The acquiescence of the public may be manifested by omission of infringing acts when the patentee makes and uses the invention, by general acceptance of licenses and payment of substantial fees, by extensive manufacture, many licenses, settlement of prior suits, and general recognition by the trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nominal royalties or licenses without consideration afford no indication of public acquiescence. Acceptance by infringers of licenses rather than contesting the patent is strong evidence. Cases: Grover & Baker Sewing Mach. Co.; Hat Sweat Mfg. Co. v. Davis Sewing Mach. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntariness requirement for acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: The submission must be voluntary; there is no acquiescence where the monopoly is constantly invaded or the rights of its owner are respected only under the compulsion of adverse judgments or continual injunctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret use or use only on the inventor's own premises that does not attract public notice does not constitute an assertion of right in which the public can acquiesce. If the invention is without utility and the public are convinced it is worthless, passive indifference indicates no public recognition. Cases: Orr v. Littlefield; Potter v. Muller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of acquiescence is measured by degree, duration, and utility
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of acquiescence as proof of validity is measured by the degree and duration of the public's submission and restraint, and by the utility of the invention and the number of persons affected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No fixed period establishes sufficiency; length required depends on how widely useful the invention is, how complete the acquiescence, and whether the public had opportunity to know and deliberate. Mere lapse of time without other facts shows no acquiescence. Examples: an eight-year exclusive possession affecting many persons may be enough; one year is usually too short.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence cannot be inferred from secret or non-public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentee alone employs the invention in secret or on his own premises, without competition or attracting public notice, there is no right asserted in which the public or an individual can acquiesce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public must have had an opportunity to become acquainted with the merits and asserted rights; secret manufacture or non-notorious use does not create public acquiescence. Cases: Orr v. Littlefield; discussions of public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquiescence limited by scope and notice of claimed invention (reissues/new claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquiescence in an original patent avails the plaintiff on a re-issue only for the same precise invention; a re-issue containing claims not in the original patent is treated as a new patent for purposes of acquiescence and public acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the public had no notice of the new claim in the reissue, prior acquiescence in the original patent cannot be construed as acquiescence to the new claims. Cases: Irwin v. McRoberts; commentary on reissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative weight: judgments vs public acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Public acquiescence is of less weight than a judgment; judgments confined to the issues litigated are stronger, while acquiescence is an admission as to all conceivable objections but is inferior because potential defenses may be unknown without litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquiescence is usually next in weight to judgments and can be strengthened by prior judgments even in coordinate or lower courts. Cases: McWilliams Mfg. Co. v. Blundell; Potter v. Whitney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions and conduct of defendant as evidence of validity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where judgments or public acquiescence are lacking, the defendant's conduct may furnish sufficient evidence: failure to deny validity in an answer is an admission; past acts may estop defendant; compromise after litigation, express contracts, covenants, and admissions of infringement can all support validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include verbal admissions and promises to desist, covenants not to infringe, compromise after expensive litigation, taking licenses and acting under them, and a defendant's ownership/office relationships with the patentee. Cases: Morse Fountain Pen Co. v. Esterbrook; Goodyear v. Railroad; Steam Gauge & Lantern Co. decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by license, covenant, assignment, or prior conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: A party who has entered into contracts acknowledging validity, taken licenses and acted under them, induced acquisition of a patent, or been a part-owner/officer enjoying patent benefits may be estopped from denying the patent's validity on a motion for injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will hold licensees, former owners, officers who enjoyed benefits, or those who agreed for valuable consideration to cease manufacture bound by their previous conduct. Cases: Parker v. McKee; Time Telegraph Co. v. Carey; Steam Gauge & Lantern Co. v. Ham Mfg. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominal licenses and payments do not show public acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Licenses issued and received on nominal royalties, or without consideration, afford no indication of public acquiescence to the validity of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment of substantial fees or manifest sacrifice of interest (paying for licenses) is necessary to infer conviction of the patent's validity. Case: Grover & Baker Sewing Mach. Co. commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of plaintiff's title (ownership) for injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must establish legal or equitable title to the patent alleged to be infringed; courts require a higher degree of certainty for title than for validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If legal title, the instruments or certified copies disclosing precise condition of ownership must be produced; if equitable interest, prove by written contract or parol testimony of facts and circumstances creating it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof of intended infringement required
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must satisfy the court that the defendant intends to make, use, or sell, or to authorize or profit by the manufacture, use, or sale, of some device or process that infringes the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity may be shown by prior judgments establishing identity, by possession or control of alleged infringing articles allowing inspection and comparison, or by other evidence the plaintiff can obtain. Courts may inspect devices personally and determine substantial agreement. Cases: many cited (Brooks v. Miller; Pullman v. B. & O. R. R.; White v. Harris & Sons).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection and comparison of devices as acceptable proof of infringement at preliminary stage
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention is an instrument and the defendant has the alleged infringing articles, the court may personally inspect and compare them and determine their substantial agreement or dissimilarity without further proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In many cases of simple mechanisms, bare inspection of the two machines is often sufficient to show infringement for the purposes of a preliminary injunction. Prior adjudications on identity, when available, may be offered. Cases: Crowell v. Harlow; Esterbrook Steel Pen Mfg. Co.; Morse Fountain Pen Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each motion for injunction requires fresh determination of intent/infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: An injunction must be determined anew upon each motion, even though the validity of the patent may have been sustained in prior judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior judgments on patent validity may settle questions adjudicated in previous cases, but the question of infringement or intended infringement on a new motion is considered afresh. Cases: Hammerschlag Mfg. Co. v. Judd; Goodyear Dental Vulcanite Co. v. Evans.
